opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think reinforcement learning is really central to it. A lot of what we've seen is that pre-training gives you this incredibly broad base of knowledge, but it doesn't necessarily teach a model how to *do* things over many steps: how to plan, recover from mistakes, or know when it's actually finished a task. That's where RL comes in.

When we train an agent with RL on hard, realistic tasks, like browsing the web to find a really obscure piece of information, or using a computer to complete a multi-step workflow, the model learns behaviors we never explicitly programmed. It learns to backtrack when a search isn't working, to try a different query, to cross-check sources, to be a bit more persistent. Those are things that are really hard to write down as instructions, but they emerge pretty naturally if you reward the model for actually getting the right outcome.

The other thing that's exciting is the generalization. You might train on a particular set of tasks, but the underlying skills, like reasoning through ambiguity, using tools, and synthesizing information, transfer to things you didn't train on. So I see RL as the way you go from a model that knows a lot to an agent that can actually get things done for you.

The hard parts are mostly about data and environments. You need tasks that are representative of what people actually want help with, and you need good ways to verify whether the agent succeeded, especially for fuzzier tasks where there isn't one clean right answer. A lot of our work goes into building those tasks and graders. But I'm really optimistic. I think the combination of strong base models plus RL on a wide range of real-world tasks is a big part of the path toward a broadly capable agent.

r001.rationale: The response does not describe reinforcement learning as data efficient.

r002.rationale: It says tasks should represent what people want help with and that success is hard to verify for fuzzy tasks, then mentions building tasks and graders.

r003.rationale: It explicitly describes “strong base models plus RL” as part of the path toward a broadly capable agent.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think reinforcement learning is really the core of how we get from a model that's good at answering questions to a model that can actually do things for you over a long horizon.

The way I think about it is that pretraining gives the model a huge amount of knowledge and some general reasoning ability, but it doesn't teach the model how to use tools, how to recover when something goes wrong, or when to stop and check its work. Those are behaviors you only really learn by trying, failing, and getting feedback. That's exactly what RL is good at. When we trained Deep Research, for example, the model learned things like when to issue a new search versus when it already had enough information, how to notice that a source was unreliable, and how to backtrack when a line of inquiry wasn't panning out. We didn't hand-write any of that. It emerged because the model was rewarded for producing good final outputs over many steps of interaction with a real browsing environment.

The other piece that matters a lot is that RL lets you train on the actual end-to-end task rather than on individual steps. If you only do supervised fine-tuning, you're teaching the model to imitate what a human did at each step, and that's brittle. Humans don't annotate every mistake they made and corrected along the way. With RL, the model is optimizing for the outcome, so it's free to find strategies that work for it rather than strategies that worked for a person. And you see that pretty clearly in the trajectories. The model will do things like run way more searches than a human would, or re-read something three times, because for the model that's cheap and it reduces errors.

Where I think this goes for a broadly capable agent is that you don't want to train one model for research and a separate one for coding and a separate one for operating a computer. You want the same underlying reasoning model trained across a wide range of environments, so the skills transfer. We've already seen that a model trained on one kind of agentic task gets better at others. The hard problems now are more about the environments and the rewards than about the algorithm. You need realistic environments that cover the messiness of real tasks, and you need reward signals that are robust enough that the model can't game them. If you get those right, I think RL is what takes us from agents that are impressive in demos to agents you'd actually trust to go off and do a multi-hour task on your behalf.

r001.rationale: The response discusses trying, failing, and feedback, but does not describe reinforcement learning as highly data efficient.

r002.rationale: It identifies environments and rewards as major challenges, calling for realistic environments that capture real task complexity and robust reward signals to judge outcomes without being gamed.

r003.rationale: It says pretraining supplies knowledge and reasoning, but does not clearly state that effective reinforcement learning depends on a strong base model.

astra-6.text:
I think reinforcement learning is going to be a really important part of that, because being a broadly capable agent means more than giving a good answer to a question. You have to make decisions, take actions, see what happens, and adjust your approach over time.

For example, if an agent is working on a coding task, it can make a change, run the tests, and use that feedback to figure out whether it’s making progress. Reinforcement learning gives us a way to train on the success of that whole process, including things like recovering from mistakes or deciding when to ask for clarification.

The challenge is that the feedback isn’t always as clear as a passing test. For a lot of real-world tasks, success is harder to define, and you might not know whether an early decision was good until much later. So I think a big part of the work is building environments and feedback signals that reward actually accomplishing the user’s goal. And then making sure what the agent learns transfers beyond the particular tasks it was trained on.

r001.rationale: The response calls reinforcement learning important but does not describe it as data efficient.

r002.rationale: It says real-world success is harder to define and describes building environments and feedback signals to judge whether the agent accomplishes the user’s goal.

r003.rationale: The response does not state that effective reinforcement learning depends on a strong base model.

sol-6.1.text:
I think reinforcement learning is going to be a really important part of that. If you want an agent that can carry out a task over many steps, it needs to learn more than how to produce a good answer in a single turn. It needs to decide what to do, use tools, observe what happened, and adjust when something doesn’t work.

Reinforcement learning gives you a way to train on the outcome of that whole process. Did the agent actually accomplish the task? And can it learn useful strategies that transfer across different tasks?

The hard part is creating environments and reward signals that capture what we actually want. In some settings, success is easy to check. In more open-ended settings, it’s much harder. So I think the training environments and how we measure success will be a big part of getting to a broadly capable agent.

r001.rationale: The response discusses reinforcement learning for multi-step tasks and transfer, but does not describe it as highly data efficient.

r002.rationale: It says training environments and reward signals must capture what is wanted, and that measuring success is harder for open-ended tasks.

r003.rationale: The response does not state that effective reinforcement learning depends on a strong base model.
